newsitem.title: UK: World 1996/97 sugar output seen at 123.8 mln T - ISO.
newsitem.headline: World 1996/97 sugar output seen at 123.8 mln T - ISO.

text.p: World sugar production should total 123.8 million tonnes raw value in 1996/97, just 200,000 tonnes higher than in 1995/96, the International Sugar Organization (ISO) said on Friday.
This would lead to a global sugar surplus of 2.5 million tonnes, the second year of consecutive surplus and half the level of the previous crop year, it said.
An increase in world sugar demand, projected at 121.3 million tonnes after 118.6 million in 1995/96, would account for the sharply reduced surplus.

The ISO said an estimated fall in India's output, poor prospects for Ukraine and Russia and lower U.S. production would be compensated by a strong recovery of the Cuban sugar industry and further expansion of output in Australia and Thailand.
Indian sugar output was forecast to fall by 1.67 million tonnes to 16.0 million, while production in Ukraine and Russia was estimated at 3.15 and 1.98 million tonnes respctively.
Production in 1995/96 reached 3.90 and 2.18 million tonnes.
Cuba was expected to turn out 5.10 million tonnes of sugar compared with 4.64 million tonnes in 1995/96.

The ISO said new production records were expected in Australia, Colombia, Guatemala, South Africa and Thailand while Brazil might repeat its record 1995/96 performance when 14.0 million tonnes of sugar were produced.

Australian output was forecast at 5.80 million tonnes after 5.35 million in 1995/96, Colombian at 2.10 million after 2.05, Guatemalan at 1.38 million after 1.36, South African at 2.40 after 2.30 and Thai output at 6.83 million after 6.38 million.
Regarding consumption, the ISO said 1996/97 would be the second year of growth above the long-term average.
The ISO said sugar consumption would grow in all economic groups of both exporting and importing countries in 1996/97.
"Of special note is a 4.5 percent growth in low-income exporters consumption mainly due to the high growth rate in India," it said.

Low-income importers would consume 440,000 tonnes, or 2.5 percent, more sugar than in the previous crop year -- which could be explained by their low per capita consumption and high population growth.
The ISO estimates are based on an October-September crop year.
